title: Episode 78: The Great Locomotive Chase: Andrews' Raid and the General
description:
The Great Locomotive Chase: Andrews' Raid and the General. How twenty-two Union soldiers and a civilian spy stole a Confederate train at Big Shanty, Georgia, in April 1862, leading to the most daring high-speed railway pursuit of the Civil War and the birth of the Medal of Honor. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into Andrews' Raiders.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. On the rainy morning of April 12, 1862, at the remote rail station of Big Shanty, Georgia, a daring plot unfolded that seemed torn from the pages of an adventure novel. While Confederate train crew and passengers were eating breakfast in a trackside hotel, twenty-two Union soldiers disguised in civilian clothing quietly uncoupled the steam engine 'The General' and three boxcars, threw open the throttle, and sped away north toward Chattanooga. Their mission: burn bridges, sever telegraph lines, and cut the Confederacy's vital rail artery. But they had not counted on the iron will of conductor William Fuller, who pursued them on foot, by handcar, and in reverse aboard a rival locomotive. George brings us the thrilling story of the Great Locomotive Chase.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE MASTERMIND AND THE MISSION
In the spring of eighteen sixty-two, the Union Army of the Ohio under General Ormsby Mitchel was poised to strike Chattanooga, Tennessee, the vital railway nexus connecting Confederate forces in Virginia with the deep South. To paralyze Confederate resistance, a tall, Kentucky-born civilian contraband merchant and secret agent named James J. Andrews proposed a breathtakingly audacious commando raid. Andrews planned to infiltrate two hundred miles behind Confederate lines into the heart of Georgia with twenty-three volunteer Union soldiers from three Ohio infantry regiments: the Second, Twenty-First, and Thirty-Third Ohio. Disguised in rough civilian attire and carrying concealed revolvers, the men were to slip across the lines in small groups, meet in Marietta, Georgia, board a northbound passenger train, hijack the locomotive, and race northward along the Western and Atlantic Railroad. Along the way, they would burn key wooden trestles across the swollen Chickamauga River, tear up rails, and sever telegraph wires, severing Chattanooga's communication and supply lines from Atlanta just as Mitchel's army attacked. General Ormsby Mitchel was an accomplished astronomer and West Point graduate who recognized that modern warfare would be decided by railway logistics and telegraph communication. Mitchel's plan was a masterstroke of military strategy: if Andrews could destroy the bridges across the Oostanaula and Chickamauga rivers, Confederate General Kirby Smith's forces in East Tennessee would be isolated from reinforcements, allowing Union forces to seize Chattanooga without a bloody frontal assault. Andrews was a charismatic and enigmatic figure who operated freely across Confederate lines by selling quinine, whiskey, and dry goods to southern merchants, masking his true identity as a master intelligence operative for the Union army.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE THEFT AT BIG SHANTY
On the misty morning of Saturday, April twelfth, eighteen sixty-two, the raiders boarded the morning northbound train out of Marietta. Eight miles north lay the small depot of Big Shanty—modern-day Kennesaw—a scheduled breakfast stop for passengers and crew. Big Shanty was chosen by Andrews for two reasons: it had no telegraph office, and while there was an army camp of four thousand Confederate recruits drilling beside the tracks, the morning breakfast bell offered twenty golden minutes of unsupervised distraction. Conductor William Fuller, engineer Jeff Cain, and the passengers stepped into the Lacy Hotel dining room to eat eggs and ham. Moving with stealth and military precision, Andrews and his men quietly uncoupled the passenger cars, climbed aboard the wooden cab of the wood-burning locomotive The General, and slipped into three empty boxcars. Union engineer William Knight opened the throttle valve: steam hissed, the iron wheels slipped on wet rails, and The General surged northward into the Georgia countryside before the startled Confederate camp sentries could raise an alarm. The raiders had spent days traveling in civilian disguise through torrential spring rains, sleeping in corn cribs and boarding houses while claiming to be Kentucky volunteers traveling to join the Confederate army in Atlanta. When William Knight pulled the throttle back at Big Shanty, the tremendous torque caused the drive wheels to spin wildly on the wet iron before biting, shooting a plume of sparks into the dawn air as the hijacked train accelerated away from the military camp.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE RELENTLESS CONDUCTOR PURSUES
Conductor William Fuller was a twenty-six-year-old railway man possessed of boundless stamina and fierce devotion to the Western and Atlantic line. Hearing the sudden whistle and the puff of steam from the dining table, Fuller ran outside, stunned to see his beloved locomotive disappearing down the tracks. Most men would have telegraphed for help or given up, but Fuller acted immediately: believing the engine had been stolen by deserters who would abandon it when they ran out of wood, Fuller took off running down the tracks on foot, accompanied by his engineer and a railway mechanic. Running over two miles at a sprint, Fuller reached Moon's Station, where he requisitioned a handcar operated by track maintenance workers. Pumping the heavy wooden levers frantically, Fuller and his companions pursued the speeding train, tumbling into ditches when they hit rails torn up by the raiders, but picking themselves up and continuing forward with unbreakable tenacity. Fuller's athletic pursuit became a legendary feat of physical endurance: he ran nearly three miles at top speed through trackside mud, driven by professional pride and the conviction that no foreign saboteurs would humiliate his railroad. When the handcar derailed on a missing rail near Moon's Station, Fuller was thrown into a bramble ditch, but scrambled to his feet instantly, righted the wooden car, and resumed pumping with blistered hands. Fuller companions marvelled at his ferocious drive, watching the young conductor sprint across railway trestles and leap over fallen trees with total disregard for his own safety to reclaim his stolen train.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE YONAH AND THE TEXAS
Fuller's relentless pursuit soon found iron muscle. Reaching Etowah, Fuller commandeered an old iron-working engine named The Yonah, steaming northward at sixty miles an hour to Kingston, where Andrews and his raiders were dangerously delayed on a siding waiting for scheduled southbound freight trains. Narrowly escaping Kingston before Fuller arrived, Andrews continued northward, cutting telegraph wires and prying up iron rails with iron crowbars. But Fuller was closing the gap: at Adairsville, Fuller abandoned The Yonah and commandeered a southbound freight train pulled by a brand-new, powerful steam engine named The Texas, commanded by engineer Peter Bracken. Without taking time to turn the engine around on a turntable, Fuller ran The Texas in reverse at breakneck speed, fifty and sixty miles an hour over crooked, wet tracks, chasing The General across northwest Georgia in the most astonishing high-speed pursuit in railway history. Running a sixty-ton steam locomotive in reverse at sixty miles an hour was an act of extraordinary mechanical daring: the tender had no forward visibility, forcing Fuller to stand exposed on the swaying woodbox peering ahead through stinging rain. Engineer Peter Bracken pushed The Texas to its boiler pressure limits, bypassing scheduled station stops and waving frantic warning signals to astonished station agents as the locomotive screamed up the main line in hot pursuit. The high-speed reverse run of The Texas was an astonishing feat of steam engineering, with sparks trailing like a comet as the iron drive rods hammered the wet rails at nearly a mile a minute.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE RUNNING BATTLE IN THE RAIN
The chase became a desperate running battle through the rainy Appalachian foothills. From the cab of The General, Andrews and his engineers realized with mounting dread that a Confederate locomotive was screaming up behind them in reverse, belching black smoke and blowing its whistle. The raiders knocked out the end wall of their rear boxcar, dropping wooden cross-ties and heavy iron rails onto the tracks behind them to derail their pursuers. But Fuller, standing bravely on the tender of The Texas as it plunged backward at terrifying speeds, spotted the obstructions, kicking ties from the rails with his boots while Bracken reversed steam to avoid catastrophe. At the Oostanaula River bridge near Resaca, Andrews attempted to burn the covered wooden span, setting fire to one of their boxcars and uncoupling it on the bridge. But the persistent spring drizzle soaked the timbers, and Fuller's engine simply pushed the smoking car ahead of it onto a siding, keeping the railway intact. The running battle became a test of nerve and ingenuity between two master engineers: Knight pushed The General to its mechanical limits while Andrews leaned from the boxcar door throwing ties onto the track, while Fuller stood on the cowcatcher of The Texas kicking obstructions away at fifty miles an hour. The soaked covered wooden bridges resisted every attempt at ignition, as the relentless rain quenched the flames before the heavy timber arches could catch. The rainy Georgia woods echoed with the sound of snapping cross-ties and squealing brake shoes as the two iron giants screamed past rural whistle-stops in an unprecedented high-speed duel.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE ABANDONMENT AND THE MANHUNT
By one o'clock in the afternoon, after eighty-seven miles of relentless pursuit, The General's fuel and water were completely exhausted. The boiler pressure gauge dropped to zero, and the engine ground to a wheezing halt two miles north of Ringgold, Georgia, barely twenty miles from Chattanooga. Realizing the game was up, Andrews gave the final order: 'Jump and scatter, every man for himself!' The twenty-two exhausted raiders leaped from the cars into the wet woods, scattering into the ravines and briar thickets of the Chickamauga Valley. But within days, Confederate cavalry, bloodhounds, and armed civilian posses combed the countryside, capturing all twenty-two raiders and James Andrews. Held in a foul subterranean dungeon in Chattanooga, Andrews and seven of his soldiers were tried by Confederate military court-martial as unlawful spies, sentenced to death, and hanged in Atlanta in June eighteen sixty-two, facing the scaffold with extraordinary courage and dignity. The capture of the raiders unleashed a furious Confederate manhunt across north Georgia, with cavalry troops and local bloodhound packs combing every ravine between Ringgold and the Tennessee river. Held in irons in the squalid military prison in Atlanta, James Andrews maintained exemplary composure, writing touching farewell letters to his fiancée in Kentucky before being led to the gallows at Peachtree Creek, mourned even by his Confederate captors for his courage.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE BIRTH OF THE MEDAL OF HONOR
The surviving raiders endured harrowing months in Confederate prisons until eight staged a daring daylight escape from an Atlanta jail, while the remaining six were formally exchanged in March eighteen sixty-three. When the survivors arrived in Washington, D.C., Secretary of War Edwin M. Stanton and President Abraham Lincoln received them at the War Department with profound admiration. Congress had recently established a new decoration for extraordinary battlefield heroism: the Medal of Honor. On March twenty-fifth, eighteen sixty-three, Secretary Stanton personally pinned the very first Medal of Honor in American history onto the jacket of nineteen-year-old raider Jacob Parrott, followed by his surviving comrades. Today, The General is proudly preserved at the Southern Museum of Civil War and Locomotive History in Kennesaw, while The Texas rests at the Atlanta History Center. Their iron boilers and brass bells stand as silent monuments to the daring Union raiders and the iron-willed conductor who clashed in the greatest locomotive chase the world has ever known. The Medal of Honor ceremony in Secretary Stanton's office marked the official birth of the nation's highest award for military valor, establishing a sacred tradition of honoring selfless bravery in the service of the republic. Jacob Parrott and his surviving comrades became celebrated heroes of the Union cause, their daring eighty-seven-mile race through Confederate Georgia remembered forever as one of the most thrilling chapters in American military history.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Great Locomotive Chase proved that bravery on the iron rails could inspire a nation and give birth to the Medal of Honor. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we journey to the north Georgia mountains for the historic Dahlonega Gold Rush of 1828.
